pages.title: Waltz's Theory of International Politics (1979)
pages.summary: Kenneth Waltz, the Detente Realist, wrote Theory of International Politics (1979) to defend realism as timeless wisdom after superpower cooperation between 1962 and 1975, such as the Partial Test Ban Treaty 1964, NPT 1969 and Helsinki Accord 1975. His methodology is structuralism, under which structures constrain the choices of actors.

pages.title: Waltz: anarchy, hierarchy, capabilities, nuclear weapons
pages.summary: Anarchy is the structure of international politics and hierarchy of domestic politics, and functional differentiation is absent internationally because all states perform the same roles. Capabilities of great powers shape politics, and Waltz supports nuclear proliferation because nuclear weapons prevent direct superpower confrontation.

pages.title: Waltz's scientific claim; Mearsheimer's context
pages.summary: Waltz calls Morgenthau's human-nature method unscientific because human nature is unpredictable, while his own analysis of structure is scientific. Mearsheimer, a post-Cold War realist, wrote The Tragedy of Great Power Politics (2001) to restore realism against liberalism and predicts possible US-China war because China is revisionist.

pages.title: Defensive versus offensive realism: purpose of power
pages.summary: Waltz (defensive) and Mearsheimer (offensive) are both structural realists who see power struggle as permanent, but differ on why states need power and how much. For Waltz the purpose of power is defence, since mindless power seeking makes others insecure and invites their combined opposition.

pages.title: Security maximisers versus power maximisers
pages.summary: For Waltz states are security maximisers who acquire only as much power as security needs. For Mearsheimer, as for Morgenthau, power is both means and end, since only hegemony gives security and the ability to alter the rules, so no amount of power is enough and offence is better than defence.

pages.title: Mearsheimer's options towards rising powers
pages.summary: Waltz finds balance of power desirable, while Mearsheimer prefers preponderance of power rather than balance. Depending on circumstances he suggests bait and bleed, blood letting and buck passing for an existing hegemon facing revisionist powers.

pages.title: Neo-classical realism, critics of structural realism, constructivism
pages.summary: Neo-classical realists Fareed Zakaria and Randall Schweller combine structure-level and actor-level analysis, so the personalities of decision makers matter and foreign policy shows continuity and change. Structural realism is criticised by seven schools, and social constructivism (Onuf, Wendt) began with Onuf's The World of Our Making.

pages.title: Constructivism: Vico, Kant and Wendt on anarchy
pages.summary: Constructivism arose because the sudden end of the Cold War showed that people lived in a world of imagination, and it draws on Vico and Kant, for whom knowledge is filtered through glasses. Wendt argues that anarchy is a construction of realists and that anarchy is what states make of it.

pages.title: Constructivist ideas and postmodern critique of realism
pages.summary: The notes say conflict arises from lack of communication and harmful ideas rather than conflict of interest, and that states are not prisoners of anarchy but constructed it in a specific way. Postmodernists (Lyotard, Foucault, Derrida) challenge claims of objectivity and call realism a discourse, and Richard Ashley's work questions realist reading of anarchy.

pages.title: Richard Ashley on anarchy as problematique
pages.summary: Ashley argues that absence of world government does not in itself lead to security dilemma and power struggle. They arise because anarchy is interpreted in a specific way, which affirms the realist view and rests on problematic inclusions and exclusions.

pages.title: English School and feminist critique of realism
pages.summary: Hedley Bull's Anarchical Society says international politics is neither complete anarchy nor complete society, as international organisations, treaties, norms and conventions have grown. Feminists find realism and the whole field masculinist, and Cynthia Enloe's Bananas, Beaches & Bases asks where the women are.

pages.title: Feminist critique, UNSC Resolution 1325, Swedish policy
pages.summary: Women are in subordinate roles, exploited in fruit plantations and tourism and excluded from decision making, and Ann J. Tickner says realist security undermines human and women's security. UN Security Council resolution 1325 recognises women's role in peace and security, and Sweden became the first country to adopt a feminist foreign policy.

pages.title: Swedish feminist foreign policy and Hillary Doctrine
pages.summary: Swedish Foreign Minister Margot Wallstrom's feminist foreign policy sees women as agents of change, not just victims, and aims at protecting human rights, meaning women's rights. The Hillary Doctrine makes women's rights integral to US foreign policy, especially in the Middle East, and a margin note flags Nirupama Rao's article on feminist foreign policy in South Asia.

flashcards.front: Why did Kenneth Waltz write Theory of International Politics (1979)?
flashcards.back: Cooperative actions between superpowers from 1962 to 1975 (Partial Test Ban Treaty 1964, NPT 1969, Helsinki Accord 1975) questioned realism. Waltz defended it as timeless wisdom through structuralism, in which structures constrain actors' choices.

flashcards.front: Why does Waltz call his realism scientific, and what structure does he identify?
flashcards.back: He builds realism on analysis of structure rather than the actor, because Morgenthau's human-nature basis is unpredictable and so non-scientific. The structure is anarchy, versus hierarchy in domestic politics, with no functional differentiation and capabilities of great powers shaping outcomes.

flashcards.front: How do defensive and offensive realism differ on the purpose and amount of power?
flashcards.back: Waltz's states are security maximisers who acquire only as much power as security needs. Mearsheimer's states are power maximisers who seek hegemony, with no amount of power enough and offence better than defence.

flashcards.front: What options does Mearsheimer suggest to an existing hegemon facing a rising or revisionist power?
flashcards.back: Depending on circumstances: bait and bleed, blood letting, or buck passing. He prefers preponderance of power over the balance of power that Waltz finds desirable.

flashcards.front: How do neo-classical realists differ from structural realists?
flashcards.back: Fareed Zakaria and Randall Schweller argue for both structure-level and actor-level analysis. Since it matters who takes foreign policy decisions, personalities are studied, and foreign policy shows continuity as well as change.

flashcards.front: What is Alexander Wendt's constructivist view of anarchy?
flashcards.back: He says anarchy is a construction of realists, who interpret the absence of common government as leading to security dilemma. Anarchy is what states make of it, and states are not prisoners of anarchy.

flashcards.front: How does Richard Ashley challenge the realist reading of anarchy?
flashcards.back: He says absence of world government does not in itself cause security dilemma and power struggle. They follow because anarchy is interpreted in a specific way, which affirms realism and rests on problematic inclusions and exclusions.

flashcards.front: What is Hedley Bull's concept of anarchical society?
flashcards.back: International politics is neither complete anarchy nor complete society but lies in the middle, as international organisations, treaties, norms and conventions grow. It takes a progressive view of human beings and international politics.

flashcards.front: What changes has the feminist school influenced in international politics?
flashcards.back: UN Security Council resolution 1325 recognises women's essential role in peace and security and their historical exclusion from decision making. Sweden became the first country to adopt a feminist foreign policy, and the Hillary Doctrine makes women's rights part of US foreign policy.

answers.question: Distinguish defensive realism of Kenneth Waltz from offensive realism of Mearsheimer, bringing out why states want power and how much.
answers.intro: Waltz and Mearsheimer are both structural realists who accept the timeless wisdom of realism and see power struggle under anarchy as permanent. They differ on the purpose for which states need power and on how much power states require.
body: Waltz wrote Theory of International Politics (1979) after superpower cooperation such as the Partial Test Ban Treaty, NPT and Helsinki Accord, while Mearsheimer wrote The Tragedy of Great Power Politics (2001) after liberal cooperation challenged realism.

For Waltz the purpose of power is defence, and states are security maximisers. Mindless power seeking makes others insecure and invites their combined opposition, so states should acquire only the power security requires. He also supports nuclear proliferation because nuclear weapons stop the two superpowers confronting each other directly.

For Mearsheimer, like Morgenthau, power is both means and end, and states are power maximisers seeking hegemony. A state is secure only with a clear gap from challengers, and power lets it alter the rules; no amount is enough.

He holds offence better than defence, with failures due to miscalculation, and suggests bait and bleed, blood letting or buck passing; he predicts US-China war because China is revisionist, while Waltz prefers balance of power.
scholars: The Tragedy of Great Power Politics (2001)
answers.conclusion: Both theories explain enduring great power rivalry, but they predict different behaviour: restraint for the defensive realist, expansion for the offensive realist. Their value lies in framing how states such as the US and China may act under anarchy.

answers.question: Critically examine how constructivism, postmodernism, the English School and feminism challenge the realist understanding of anarchy and international politics.
answers.intro: Structural realism treats anarchy as the structure that produces security dilemma and power struggle. Constructivism, postmodernism, the English School and feminism challenge this, arguing that anarchy, objectivity and the field itself rest on constructed ideas.
body: Wendt says anarchy is a construction of realists, what states make of it, and states are not prisoners of anarchy. Onuf, Vico and Kant support the idea that knowledge is filtered through glasses, so conflict stems from lack of communication and ideas.

Postmodernists (Lyotard, Foucault, Derrida) challenge objectivity and scientific claims and call realism a discourse. Richard Ashley adds that absence of world government does not itself cause security dilemma; anarchy is interpreted in a specific way that affirms realism.

Hedley Bull's Anarchical Society says politics is neither complete anarchy nor complete society, since international organisations, treaties, norms and conventions have grown. It takes a progressive view of both human beings and international politics.

Feminists call the field masculinist: Cynthia Enloe asks where the women are, and Ann J. Tickner says realist security undermines human and women's security. Their influence shows in UN resolution 1325, Sweden's feminist foreign policy under Margot Wallstrom and the Hillary Doctrine.
answers.conclusion: These critiques do not remove realism's explanatory power, but they show that anarchy, security and power depend on interpretation and on who is included. Realism now has to answer for its assumptions rather than treat them as given.
